speechtext:
(Whenever you are in the city, we shall be pleased to have you call.)
Catch on to the words ' Yours in the good cause.' Now, who is Mr. Perry, and what do we know about him? He has been a great actor who has played some very important parts on various political stages, always for the Liberal party, not only in Manitoba, but in Saskatchewan, and in order that the House may understand how he plays his part on these political stages, I will recall just one instance out of many which will be sufficient to satisfy the House, and it should be sufficient to satisfy the Minister of Agriculture that Mr. Perry is not a man in whom he should have the utmost confidence; that is, if he wishes to play the game of politics fairly. It will be remembered that there was an election in the constituency of Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, on the 13th day of December, 1905, and the Liberal party had as their candidate Mr. Tyreman, and Mr. Donaldson was a candidate of the Provincial Rights party. Mr. Donaldson was recognized as much the stronger candidate, and dhe Liberals decided to beat him at any cost, and something had to be done. What was done was to call into play the Grit machine, and after it was sufficiently oiled and greased it was put into operation. The first move was to select the battlefield, and if the House will take the trouble to look at the map, they will find that the constituency of Prince Albert runs far into the wilds of the north, and so the northern wilds were selected by the Grit machine for its handiwork and robbery. Mr. Moberley, the Liberal organizer, made application to returning officer Sinclair for three polls to be opened in the north, and needless to say the application was immediately granted. It was understood that Mr. Donaldson, the provincial rights candidate, was to know nothing of it then, and in order to jockey time, Mr. Sinclair, the returning officer, rode forty miles into a little town called Shell Brook, from which the mail only leaves twice a week. On the 5th of December, after the mail had left, Mr. Sinclair, the returning officer, mailed a notice to Mr. Donaldson that there would be three polls opened up in the north, and it was absolutely impossible for Mr. Donaldson to get this notice until the 7th of December, or six days before the election.

when he could not possibly get there himself or send a representative on that short notice to protect these three polls. The next move was for Mr. Sinclair, the returning officer, to select three deputy returning officers and he procured the efficient services of a Mr. McLeod, a Mr. Neil-son, and a Mr. Sutherland, and they started on the northern trip. After journeying for some time they came to a desolate and lonely spot, and they concluded that they had travelled far enough, so they also concluded that it was a most ideal place to do the work they had gone out to do, and to set the Grit machine working. Therefore, they made a camp fire and sat down. They had some liquid refreshments and although the narrative does not say what foodstuffs they used, it is supposed it was the standard Grit machine grulb namely pickled pigs' feet and beer, and no doubt'they smoked the Laurier brand of cigars from the good ship * Arctic.'
After having a hearty supper, they decided that they would go to work. The first thing to be done was to make a list. So they got their pencils and paper out, and sat down and began putting down all the names thev could think of. Finally their mental ability, and capacity of thinking of names became exhausted; yet they had not in their opinion quite sufficient names on the list to defeat the provincial rights candidate. At that moment, fortunately for Mr. Tyreman, but unfortunately for Mr. Donaldson, a rabbit went jumping by. The incident suggested the name of a new family that they might register, so they began registering the Rabbit family. They entered on the list Tommy Rabbit, Jack Rabbit, and I was told Jennie Rabbit, and all the Test of the Rabbit family. After they had got the Rabbit family all Entered up, they counted up the list, and they found 151 names on the list, and they concluded, after a little consultation, that that was sufficient to do the trick. The next move was to open the polls. So they unlocked the ballot boxes* took out the poll book, took out the pad of ballots, and they got up, I suppose, behind the back log for a table, and began work. Now, Mr. Speaker, can you imagine the scene? Just imagine that you see those men at work, away up there in the north, at a poll constituted as I have said, and- imagine you see Tommy Rabbit, and Jack Rabbit, and Jennie Rabbit, stepping into the poll announcing their names and demanding ballots; and there Mr. Sutherland, and Mr. Macleod, and Mr. Neilson hand out the ballots, and the Rabbits go back and mark them, fold them, and come back and drop them into the ballot box. Then I suppose they got their usual glass of beer and pigs' feet, and cigar, and went home to await the Teturns of the poll. After
they had got the 151 ballots in the box, the time arrived' to close the poll. The poll was closed. The ballot boxes were unlocked, the marked ballots taken out and counted. It was found that there were 151 ballots, and every one of them had voted right, they were all marked for Mr. Tyreman,' the Liberal 'candidate.. VThetn, they gathered up their traps, and whatever little provision they had left, and started back to Prince Albert. When they arrived at Prince Albert they handed in their ballot box and made the solemn declaration to the returning officer, Mr. Sinclair, and he declared Mr. Tyreman, the Liberal candidate, elected by about 60 majority. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is the way that incident occurred^ But Mr. Donaldson decided that he was not going to stand for all that. He felt that Jre was entitled to some degree of justice. So he immediately took action against the three returning officers. They were taken to court, and were fined as follows:	Mr. Sutherland, deputy, Mr. Macleod, another deputy, and Mr. Neilson, $200 each, and Mr. Moberly, $100. That quieted things for a time. But Mr. Donaldson was not satisfied with that. He then instituted proceedings against Mr. Sinclair, the returning officer. The charge he made against Mr. Sinclair was conspiring to defraud in the matter of the list. This somewhat alarmed the Liberal machine, and the Liberals throughout the country, and immediateb'' they advised the deputy returning officers to skip out. After they were supplied with the necessary cash, and the assurance that they would be looked after, the deputies went across into the United States. And now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the point where I want to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the beautiful letters that were written by his friend Mr. Perry, in whom he has every confidence, and see what the House and even the minister himself think of them. These poor fellows were in the United States for a time. They were running short of cash, and they were anxious to get back. They had to be administered to, and Mr. Perry administered comfort to their souls, and cash in their pockets. I will read to the House extracts from some of his letters to Mr. Neilson. I hold in my hand facsimiles of all the letters that passed between Mr. Neilson, Mr. Perry, Mr. Sutherland, and the rest of the gang, so that they cannot be disputed. Some of them are rather spicy. This is from one dated June 10:
Nothing new in. the Sinclair case. Appeal to be heard by full court at Calgary, July
^Moberly should have requested protection of court; as it is, it seems there is nothing for him to do but plead guilty.
Tories threatening further prosecution.

I have heard it said that the missing deputies would he as well to keep out of sight. I think this is undoubtedly correct.
On June 11th, he writes further:
Ere this reaches you, no doubt you will have heard that Moberly was fined $100.
Tories are talking of other prosecutions,, and are, of course, pleased with the results so far.
Prudence would, I should judge, suggest to the absent deputies that their safety lies in their remaining away.
These were written by Mr. Perry to Mr. Neilson. Here is another one:
Box 723,
Regina, Oct. 24, 1906.
Dear Mr. Neilson,-I write to inform you that the Tories are still threatening. You see if they lose the case against Sinclair it will make them hostile, while if they win they will be in good shape to prosecute further. That is the way they look at it, so I would advise extreme caution. I shall try to keep you advised. Am going up to Prince Albert shortly to see how things look. The 'Standard' here last night published a story that if the case went against Sinclair, he was going to squeal, but I don't believe that, as he would never do anything to help the Tories, he is a sore on them. Kindly consider this as absolutely confidential and done in your interests.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) H. E. PERRY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

speechtext: On whose recommendation was Moberley appointed?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I cannot remember.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: As a matter of fact, they were not punished for all of these things. The facts are beyond dispute They were guilty of eight or ten offences under the Election Act. In addition to that they were guilty of the trifling offences of forgery and perjury, that is all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: The minister can understand himself: this was the case of two deputy returning officers going out and holding a poll, and returning 151 electors as having voted when there was not a single man appeared before them to vote_ at all; putting down fictitious names, putting in bogus ballots and making a solemn return under the Election _Act that these men had actually voted and that a poll was held and then bringing that return back and having the votes counted for one of the candidates; surely the minister can understand what the offence was.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: None of these statements were contained in the letter to which I have referred, and this is the first time I knew in any shape or form of what these men were supposed to be guilty. But I want to point out that these men had nothing to do with the census. Mr. Moberley seemed to be connected with the transaction, and in the case in court was found guilty of something, when I found he was proven guilty I sent after him" and recalled him, and refused to allow him to continue as census officer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: What is he doing now?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I do not know what he is doing, but he is not acting in connection with the census in any manner, and if I found out to-morrow he was acting, I would cancel his appointment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I do not say he lias, but I do say that as Liberal organizer in the province of Manitoba, he is sending out circulars inviting your agents to come into his office for instructions, and he was shielding these people who were guilty.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

Mr. Perry has nothing to do with the taking of the census for the Department of Agriculture. If Mr. Perry
wishes to write to a census enumerator or commissioner, I have nothing to do with it. He is not doing so with my authority; he has no authority from the department or from me to do it, and he has nothing to do with the taking of the census.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

speechtext: As far as I am concerned, Mr. Perry has no patronage of any place at all. But

speechtext: LAKE (Qu'Appelle) Mr. Speaker this is not the first time that the history of the notorious Prince Albert elections has been given in this House. It was given by myself a good many years ago, in less eloquent and picturesque language, perhaps, but with the facts substantially the same throughout. The minister must have heard it on that occasion, as I am pretty certain he was in the House, and it was notorious throughout the whole of Canada, being printed in the public press from one end of the country to the other. The main facts are that there was a conspiracy to obtain illicit votes in favour of the Liberal candidate in the Prince Albert election. Three men started out into the wilds with the avowed purpose of opening three polls. They did not open any polls at all. They went to a secluded place, opened their poll booths and filled the poll books with fictitious names.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Was that a provincial or a Dominion election?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
A provincial election. Amongst the fictitious names occurred very frequently the name of Rabbitskin. It was shown at the time that after the three deputy returning officers had exhausted the names they could recall to mind, the

ordinary -every-day names, Mr. Moberley, who was with them, -suggested that he had heard of a family of half-breeds in that neighbourhood called Rabbitskin. So they filled out a large number of the entries with the surname of Eabbitskin, with many different Christian names attached to them. Then, having filled the poll books with names, they filled the ballot boxes with bogus ballots, brought them back from the wilds into the- town -and produced 151 ballots, -sufficient to elect the Liberal candidate. The minister will remember-in fact, he remembered to-day- that Mr. Moberley, the man who was very active in connection with that affair, who acted as poll clerk, and was fined for his connection with the business, was appointed to a job in connection with the census. The minister must have understood that the case was a very bad one, because he took -summary proceeding, after the matter had been repeatedly brought to his notice in this House, to have Mt. Moberley recalled at [DOT] some expense to the country. Two of the three deputy returning officers who were concerned in this notorious business were government officials. Both of them lost their jobs. I presume that even the present administration did not consider it safe to retain them in government positions. The third was a homesteader, and the government in his case was kind enough to protect his homestead, and gran-t him an extension of leave during his enforced absence in the United States, as a fugitive from justice. The case indeed was so bad that Dr. Tyreman, who had- been declared elected by the returning officer, refused to take his seat in the legislature, and did not take hi-s seat. Subsequently the Committee on Elections and Privileges in the Local House, having exhaustively inquired into the case, awarded the seat to Mr. Donaldson, the Provincial Eights candidate. The minister speaks- of these men as having -been guilty of a trivial offence. The leader of the opposition put the matter clearly and tersely this afternoon when he declared that these deputy returning officers, who were, subsequently fugitives from justice, had been guil-ty of perjury and forgery. The minister says that he can see no connection between the Prince Albert election case and the appointment of census officials for the province of Manitoba. The connection is that M-r. Perry is iprovedi by title -corres/pondemca which has been read in the House to-day to have been guilty of conspiring to defeat the ends of justice by assisting these men to become fugitives from justice and advising them to keep out of the way. Let me -read M-r. P-erry'-s own letter, a facsimile of which was subsequently published 285
in the press of the country. This is.what Mr. Perry himself said:
Box 723,
Regina, Sask., Oct. 20, 1906.
Dear Sir,-I inclose for your information and guidance copy of ' Leader ' of this date containing complete text of judgment of the full court in the Sinclair case and which disposes of the conspiracy phase of the Prince Albert district election cases. It does not, however, dispose of the two counts against the deputy returning officers and poll clerks, viz.: Making false returns; stuffing ballot boxes; for which they are liable under sections 128 and 133 of the Territories Elections Ordinance.
Section 128 reads:-Any persons appointed as returning officer, election clerk, deputy returning officers or poll clerk, who fails to carry out any of the duties imposed by this ordinance or who contravenes any of its provisions shall be liable to a fine not exceeding $500 and costs, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding one year, or both.
Section 133 reads:-Penalties under this ordinance may be recovered on summary conviction before two justices of the peace.
The three deputies were fined on only one charge, that of not holding the polls at the proper time and place.
Moberley, a poll clerk, was fined for writing the word ' voted' after the names of parties in the poll book, his fine being $100, while that of each deputy w-as $200.
The Tories are naturally disappointed and sore over the decision of the full court, and I am informed that Moore, editor of their paper, the ' West,' and McDonald, their organizer, are going to Prince Albert the beginning of the next week.
I am -also informed on the best authority that the Tories say that any or all of the fellows who are away, will be arrested immediately on their return, which quite bears out what I have understood all along they were threatening to do.
I, therefore, cannot hold out any hope for your early return; things will settle down after a while, when the by-election is over and after the end of next session of the House. I shall be pleased to give you any further information, if possible to obtain it, and you so desire.
Yours very truly,

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

speechtext: So that by the letter of Mr. Perry himself he stands convicted of aiding and abetting the escape of criminals from justice. And yet the minister appears to treat him as quite a fit and proper representative of the Liberal party in the province of Manitoba, and apparently he sees no harm in consulting him as a representative Liberal. Well, i-f ministers of the Crown consider such men fit representatives of the great Liberal party, we are content that they should do so. The Minister of Agriculture went on to say that he had numerous recommendations, many of which were from Mr. Perry for appointments to the censu-s, but he refused to say upon whose recommendations he acted with

regard to the different cases. All the evidence, however, points to the fact that in a number of cases he acted on Perry's recommendation. At any rate the confidential circular issued by Mr. Perry, and which was read by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), shows that whether the appointments were made on the recommendation of Mr. Perry or not, it was he who was entrusted with the duty of notifying the successful candidates of their selection by the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: The enumerators were all notified toy the Department. No one else had any authority to notify them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Apparently this Liberal organizer considered that he had the authority.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: He had none.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
Allow me to read the letter which he -wrote, which will show that he acted as if the appointments came from him and from him only. This circular letter, which I am about to read, is headed:
Liberal Executive Organization Committee, Winnipeg, April 17, 1911.
Dear Sir,-Re census in federal constituency of McDonald. I beg to advise, yon that you have been recommended as enumerator for the following official census enumeration division of the above constituency:-
Then follows a typewritten slip with these words:-
61. That part of the parish of St. Charles, north of the Assinihoine river.
Mr. Perry goes on to say:
I inclose copy of rates as officially announced in the ' Canada Gazette ' of April 15, 1911, and would he pleased if within ten days you would please acknowledge reception of this letter.
Yours in the good cause,

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

speechtext:
P.S.-Whenever yon are in the city, we shall be pleased to have yon call.
Does the minister repudiate that letter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I say that Mr. Perry had no authority to give any intimation to the enumerators of their appointments. I had nothing to do with that letter and knew nothing about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: It is very strange this Liberal organizer should have known the persons who were recommended.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman must accept my statement that Mr. Perry had no authority.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
I am not disputing the statement and I take it that the minister repudiates this letter. This is a circular letter with the blanks filled in in another Mr. LAKE.
handwriting and with a slip attached in another kind of typewriting, which indicates that a number of different letters were written to a number of different individuals, and a rubber stamp is used for the signature. One cannot doubt therefore that Mr. Perry was cognizant of all those who were recommended for these appointments. Whether he was so informed by the minister or not is another question; but that he was absolutely personally cognizant of all these recommendations this letter fully establishes. It was the first notice that each person appointed had of his appointment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: The minister should explain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Then the person recommended is asked to acknowledge within ten days the receipt of the letter notifying him of his appointment. Why was he asked to do so if Mr. Perry was not in some way connected with the official recommendation? The minister repudiated the idea that the enumerators were to go to the Liberal organizer for instructions. He may say that they were not _ to go to the Liberal organizer for instructions with regard to their work as enumerators, but the postcript attached to the letter shows clearly that they were to go to the Liberal organizer foT instructions as to the side work and the canvassing they were to do in the interests of the Liberal party. I have no wish to detain the House any longer. Mr. Moberly was appointed on the recommendation of some one. On whose recommendation the minister cannot remember. Probably it was on the recommendation of Perry himself. The minister made the appointment and then subsequently had to put the public to considerable expense in order to send for this man .and get him toack from the wilds of the far north. Mr. Moberly had been convicted and fined and the time had come foT the Department or the Liberal executive to Teward him. and they apparently recommended him for this appointment in the census. This man, Perry, is convicted, according to his own letters, of endeavouring to keep fugitives from justice out of the reach of the strong arm of the law. Does the minister consider that such a person is a proper man from whom to accept any recommendations? Is he prepared to say that he did accept the recommendations of Mr. Perry for appointments as census eumerators? I pause for a reply-

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I am not ready to say that I have not accepted any of his recommendations.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
Then I hope the minister will now take steps to see that the persons

who were recommended by this man are promptly cancelled. It seems to me that these recommendations were improperly made, and I sincerely hope that this House will not endorse the action of the Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
I do not intend to take up much time, but as this is a question which affects the whole province of Manitoba, I consider it my duty to give my views with regard to it. It is a question that deserves most serious consideration. Charges have been made against a gentleman ocupying the prominent position of Liberal organizer for the province of Manitoba. This gentleman is practically repudiated by the Minister of Agriculture, yet he assumes power and authority to -write the letter that has been read by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle. (Mr. Lake) addressed to the enumerators throughout the province advising them of their appointment and asking them to call at his office for instructions, and I hold that this calls for some action by the minister who is responsible for the census. The minister says this man has no authority; he repudiates him, as I understand it. I ask him what action he is going to take. Is he going to remain silent in the face of this circular letter sent out by the Liberal OTganizer in Manitoba to the enumerators, asking them to call at this man's office. In view of the record of the Liberal organizers in Manitoba, and the experience of the Conservative party with these men, it becomes imperative for the Conservative members <of this House to discuss this matter with the minister who is responsible, for the conduct of these men. I cannot conceive that any crime could be committed by any man occupying the position this man occupies greater than the crime which has been brought home to him in relation to this Prince Albert election. It is one of the most scandalous affairs that ever took place in Canada. These men manufactured three polls where there was not one soul living. According to the history of this case over 160 ballots were made up in a little bluff. These men sat down and deliberately manufactured a list. Yet this Mr. Perry, the Liberal organizer, is the man who shielded these men from justice, and when they were fugitives from the country, this man remained at home advising them that it was dangerous for them to return, that the Tories were threatening to prosecute. This is the man who organiezs the province of Manitoba for the Liberal party. History repeats itself in regard to these organizers. We have had other cases about as bad in that province. But we thought the Liberal party had been taught a lesson and that they would hesitate before they would again employ a [DOT]man with a record as spicy as that of this 2851
man Mr. Perry. There is no question that this gentleman, in that Prince Albert elec-tion_ case, stood between these men and justice, that he shielded them, and that he was a party to the crimes they committed in relation to these ballot boxes. I do not suppose for a minute that the minister knew who this man was when he accepted his recommendation to appoint enumerators, but now that he does know, I ask him, is he going to confirm his appointment?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I certainly will not change *appointments until I find that the appointees are not worthy of their offices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I would ask the minister this question: What is he going to do in regard to this circular letter which this gentleman sent out?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Nothing whatever. The gentleman has a right to write a letter, just as the hon. gentleman himself (Mr. [DOT]Bradbury) has.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I take a very different view of this question. The minister (Mr. Fisher) is Responsible to this country for the proper taking of the census.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: He is bound to safeguard the men who take that census. Put aside the fact that this man is a Liberal organizer. It might be any other man who would write a letter of that kind addressed to the enumerators, asking them to come in for instructions-

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: May I see that letter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: It has just been read by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake).

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:

-of the above constituency No. 51, that part of the parish of St. Charles, north of the Assiniboine river.

I wish now to deal with the Prince Albert election case, and I may say to begin with that it has as much to do with the taking of the census as the Indian mutiny has. What connection it has with the census, I cannot see, and I do not believe that any sensible man can. One Sinclair and one Moberley, and some one else, away back in 1905, a few weeks after we first became a province, went out, as my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples), with his ponderous reasoning says, to watch jack-

rabits and eat pickled pigs' feet. And these men did what was wrong. The result was that two or three Liberals were coralled for having broken an election ordinance of the Northwest Territories such as it was then. They came back, they were punished. There lived in the province of Saskatchewan some of the very cleverest lawyers who are supporters of that provincial rights party; men who could have prosecuted these offenders, and if they thought they did wrong could have ensured that they were prosecuted to the hilt; men like the Hon. Frederick William Gordon Haultain, who was eight or nine years attorney general of the Northwest Territories, and who with his own pen had written the election ordinance they broke. Why didn't he, seeing that the courts of the land were open to_ every one, swing wide their doors and himself lay, or have some one else lay a complaint for forgery or perjury. Then there was Mr. J. T. Brown, now one of the judges of the Supreme Court of Saskatchewan who, had the provincial rights party been elected, would have been their attorney general no doubt, and there was every opportunity for Liberal and Conservative alike to prosecute these men to the hilt for just as serious a charge as it was possible to bring against them. There is no reflection on the Liberal party in connection with that matter. It is not the business of the Liberal party any more than of the Conservative party to prosecute men, even though they be party friends. But these men were prosecuted. They were fined by the magistrates who had been appointed by Mr. Haultain himself on the testimony produced before them such as it was. I merely mention that fact to show that there could be no suspicion surrounding their trial, and what the magistrate thought was a just punishment was meted out to them, and they bore it. Now, why is the Minister of Agriculture to be called upon to answer for all this? What connection is there between that and the appointing of some census commissioners in the province of Manitoba?
It is said by these gentlemen opposite that this man, Mr. Perry, some months afterwards, down in the city of Begina, wrote a few letters to these men telling them how the litigation was proceeding, and telling them that if they were to return they no doubt would be prosecuted, and stating that if they wished to avoid meeting a charge of that kind at that time, they had better not return within the jurisdiction of that court. There is nothing *criminal about that. I would dare to say that any lawyer would write such a letter to his client; I would dare to say that any friend would send such a letter to another friend under similar circumstances. Even
if I were not a lawyer, and not acting as solicitor, if I had a friend who wanted to know liow litigation was proceeding, would not feel that I would demean myself by giving him any information that any man in the land had to give that was present on the ground. Everybody knew these things which Mr. Perry was writing to that man, and there is absolutely no guilt resting on Mr. Perry, and there is absolutely nothing to connect him with a crime, and there is not even the slightest suspicion cast this afternoon in the remarks of gentlemen opposite that Mr. Perry knew anything about that offence before it was committed, or that he had ever dreamed of such a thing. The only cjmrge they can make is that he knew of the threatened charge afterwards, and that he did a friendly act for those who were then awav from the jurisdiction of the courts ot Saskatchewan.	.

I am pleased with that declaration of the Minister of Agriculture, and I trust that our friends opposite will read between the lines and, seeing that they are so keen on reading ' instructions/ see that there is a little instruction meant for them in that. And, I think that what the Minister of Agriculture meant is: that the Liberals are governing this country, that they make the appointments to office, that they get their recommendations where in their wisdom they think right. The ministers no doubt use their own judgment, and they seek the counsel of their friends, and if they wish it sometimes of their foes, but when it comes to the last resort I think what the Minister of Agriculture meant was that the sixty, seventy or eighty hon. gentlemen opposite should understand that for the present at least the Laurier government is governing this country and making the appointments to office. I have not heard the hon. gentleman condemn any action of that kind on the part of a minister of the Crown. I think the taking of the census is a matter that should be absolutely free from any taint or suspicion of party politics. By that I do not claim that the poiitical proclivities of the census enumerators .should be completely ignored, because I recognize that in this country we have party government, and in such appointments the party in power will always give the preference to their own political friends. With that I havp no fault to find. But when the government ignore the character of the appointees, and when they select Liberal organizers who bear unsavoury reputations *and appoint them, not only for their qualifications, but as a reward for party services of a most questionable character as has occurred in this instance, and in many instances in the past in the province of Manitoba, it is a different matter. As the hon. member for Selkirk has truly said, it is most unfortunate that the Liberal organizers in the province of Manitoba for years back have been men who have been guilty of questionable transactions which have' resulted in bringing into disrepute not only themselves but the party they represent. It is only necessary to refer to the gentleman who preceded Mr. Perry as the Liberal organizer, Mr. R. E. Leach, the author of 'the thin red line,' by which he
disfranchised a larger number of electors, and who was rewarded afterwards with an office in the Department of the Interior carrying $2,000 a year and expenses, and whose expenses have been so outrageous that the Auditor General has taken him strictly to task for them in his report of this year. It is also worthy of notice that nearly every person who worked with Mr. Leach at that time, and assisted him in disfranchising the electors, has also received a position under this government. It is only necessary to refer to Messrs. Maeleod, Neigh, Ayotte and Duggan. It seems strange that men who are guilty of acts of the most questionable character on behalf of the party are able to hold up the government and secure almost any position they ask. Now, the hon. Minister of Agriculture was not quite so frank with the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), as he should have been on Friday wThen answering his questions. In that somewhat important air which he sometimes arrogates to himself, he replied to some of the questions in the most emphatic manner. For instance, when he was asked if certain enumerators were appointed, he honestly and frankly stated that they were. When he was asked, however, who recommended them, he declined to answer, though to-day he is not nearly so reluctant to answer the question, for he did admit that Mr. Perry, the Liberal organizer, nominated some of the enumerators. To the third question, did Mr. Perry ask the enumerators to come into his office to be schooled, he most emphatically replied, no. We can all read between the lines and can realize that when Mr. Perry wrote that letter inviting the enumerators to come into his office and be schooled, he did not mean in order to count the heads for census purposes, but to school them to count political heads in order that this information might be utilized by the Liberal party in the province. This information would come in very well at this particular time, because in the province of Manitoba they are just now in the act of revising the voters' lists, in connection with which the information that could be secured by these census enumerators by turning them into party hacks would be of a most useful character. The information would also be most useful to this government when the redistribution takes place a few months hence, and in the_election that is expected to take place in the near future. April the 17th of this year. The hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) has asked what connection had' the Prince Albert election to do with the selection of enumerators ifor Manitoba. Well, if the Prince Albert election has no direct connection with the selection of enumerators for Manitoba, it has a very direct connection with the gentleman through whose hands aparently these enumerators are being appointed, I refer to Mr. Perry. According to the correspondence read tonight, this man Perry stood in a very unenviable light indeed in connection with the shielding these fugitives from justice, who had to flee from the country because of their doings in the Prince Albert election when working the Liberal machine. That was one of the most disgraceful episodes in the political history of this country. Fancy these deputy returning officers and poll clerks being sent away out north to hold polls hundreds of miles from Prince Albert. They did not go within a hundred miles of the places where they were to hold the polls, but they sat down on the prairie, took out their poll books and poll boxes, and wrote in the poll books the names of 150 fictitious individuals-lamong them, as my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) has said the Rabbit family predominated-and they stuffed the ballot boxes with 150 ballots, every one of which was marked in favour of the Liberal candidate. And they came back to Prince Albert with their boxes and their poll books and hailed the result as a great victory in the far north for the Liberal candidate, morally and otherwise. They made out their false returns. Forgery and perjury are none too strong names to characterize their actions. When arrested and brought before the court, who was it appeared to prosecute them and who appeared in their behalf? Instead of the Mr. ROCHE.
Dominion government prosecutor appearing before the court to see that justice was done, he appeared in their defence. They pleaded guilty and were fined. The deputy returning officers were fined $.200 each and the poll clerks $100 each for having stuffed the ballot boxes land made false returns. The fines 'were paid by a clerk in the Crown prosecutors office. Where did the money come from? I think we -.need not stretch our imagination very much to say that it could have come from no other source than the Liberal campaign fund. But when recount of the ballots took place, after these men had been fined and after it was proven that 150 ballots were fictitious, the judge holding the recount, counted evejy one of these as legitimate. That may have been technically within the law, but there is not a man within the sound of my voice, be he Liberal or Conservative who will not siay it was travesty of justice.
After the 'trial some of these deputy returning officers made themselves scarce. They fled south of the boundary line, and then this correspondence took place between Perry and these fugitives from justice, which the hon. member for Moose jaw (Mr. Knowles) looks upon as so innocent that he, as a lawyer, would do it fox any of his clients. Well, I do not think the hon. gentleman will find his ethics endorsed by other practitioners at the bar; but in any event Mr. Perry was not acting as a lawyer for these men, but as the head of the Liberal machine in that province, as the Liberal organizer, and be was accessory to those offences, after if not, before, because he was doing his best to keep these men out of the country lest there should be still greater rascalities unearthed if they remained or reappeared on the scene.
I do not propose to go through all this correspondence, but wish to refer to a few paragraphs in this correspondence which the hon. member for Moosejaw tells us was of such an innocent character. In the letter of June 10, I find these paragraphs :
Tories threatening further prosecution.
I have heard it said that the missing deputies would he as well to keep out of sight, I think this is undoubtedly correct.
This is the gentleman against whom the hon. member for Moosejaw says there has not been found anything wrong by reason of anything that transpired in that election or subsequently. The following day Perry wrote again:
Tories are talking of other prosecutions and are, of course, pleased at the results so far.
Prudence would, I should judge, suggest to the absent deputies that their safety lies in remaining away.
This is taken from correspondence between Perry and Neilson, and Perry was

not then writing as a lawyer to a client, but as the Liberal organizer advising these people to stay away until the trouble had blown over, as they would be subject to more prosecutions, should they Teappear on the scene.
Let me quote one more paragraph out of a letter written by Perry on October, the 4th, to Neilson, who acted as deputy returning officer:
The 'Standard' here last night published a story that if the case went against Sinclair, he was going to squeal.
Squeal about what? Squeal on whom? Evidently there was something which had not yet been brought to light and which Perry was afraid might come out if further prosecutions took place. But he expresses his confidence in the returning officer Sinclair by saying:
But I do not believe that, as he would never do anything to help the Tories, he is too sore on them. Kindly consider this as absolutely confidential and. done in your interests.
This came from Perry who evidently had the ear of the Department of Agriculture, if not the minister, and who assumed the responsibility of sending out a circular under the seal of confidence to his appointee notifying him of his appointment and inviting him to his office on the first opportunity. In a letter written on October 20th, 1906, Perry goes on to say to Neilson:
I am also informed on the best authority that the Tories say that any or all of the fellows who are away will be arrested immediately on their return, which quite bears out what I have understood all along they were intending to do.
I, therefore, cannot hold out any hope for your early return. Things will settle down after awhile when the by-election is over, and after the end of next session of the House. I shall be pleased to give you any further information if possible to obtain it and you so desire.
All through this correspondence, Perry as Liberal organizer, is trying to keep these men, who perpetrated these frauds on the electors, out of the country lest further exposures might result, should they return to the disadvantage of the Liberal party.
In connection with that election, I remember a memorable saying of the Prime Minister of that province (Mr. Scott). When the returns were coming in that evening from the thickly settled portions of the province and they were going against the government, Mr. Scott, in addressing his audience, said: ' Wait; until you hear from the back townships.' Evidently he knew what these returns from the back townships would be and was not ignorant of what was transpiring in that portion of the country.
It is only necessary to look at the signature to the circular to show what connection there was between this government and the Liberal organizer. The Minister of Agriculture asks us to believe that any person might send out such a circular as that. Well, I wonder if a Conservative organizer sent out a letter like that, what the minister would have done. I fancy he would very soon have called him down. He would soon take him to task for arrogating to himself the authority to notify the enumerators as to their pay, as to the positions to which they were appointed, as to the territory they were supposed to cover, and practically to extend to them an invitation to come in and be schooled in his office. And when he winds up his letter ' Yours in the good cause ' he emphasizes the fact that it was not for the census alone that he was writing, but rather that he might use them as political partisans-to count heads for the party as 'well as for the census. I think the minister (Mr. Fisher) should accept the motion of the hon. member for Macdonald. The minister says that for fifteen years past they have recognized that public office is a public trust. They have taken a very peculiar way to exhibit that to the country, if we may judge them by the appointments they have made. Leach, Mr. Perry, Ayotte, Neigh, McLeod, Duggan-all these men who figured in these scandalous transactions of the past have been provided for by one member of the government or another. Ingram, the organizer who tampered with the lists on election day, and who was also Liberal organizer for a time-I do not think he is now; I believe that Mr. Perry is the organizer-has also been provided for. I say the minister takes a peculiar way of showing his belief that public office is a public trust when he refuses to receive the motion put forward by the member for Macdonald. I think that one of his first duties in view of what has been brought to his attention to-day is to call Mr. Perry down in short order and show that he is really in earnest in saying that Mr. Perry has done this without authority. Mr. Perry should be notified to that effect, and that duty devolves upon the Minister of Agriculture, because he is the one whom this parliament will hold responsible.

Reid, and the minister may possibly tell us what connection he has with the western district in reference to the census taking. I see it stated that:
J. C. Macpherson, special census commissioner, is in London, and will be here for the next five days, instructing the census commissioners who have been appointed to supervise the census taking in this western peninsula. To-day, Mr. Macpherson met the commissioners from Lambton, Essex and Kent county.
I find in another column of the same paper the following:
Liberal club to approve the list.
Commissioner Scateherd presents his census appointments for revision.
Says he gave the list to George M. Reid.
Majority of forty appointments find they have not the qualifications.
Mr. Scateherd selected the brightest and best men according to his judgment, but he had to present their names to a committee in the city of London, the head of which was Mr. George M. Reid, whom surely the minister remembers in connection with the election frauds of years gone by, and how he was brought before the courts in Toronto. Yet he is still seen strongly in evidence in the western districts of Ontario in handling the affairs of the Census Department, a department, I am sure the minister must agree with me in saying, that can best be dealt with by taking it out of politics altogether. But let me read something that this paper has to say in reference to this matter:
Many young men of this city who made application for a position as census enumerators will be disappointed. Most of them will not secure the appointment.
E. W. Scateherd, who is to have charge of the taking of the census, received something like 105 applications, and practically appointed the forty men required to do the work.
A committee of three of the Liberal politicians of the city was appointed to go over the appointments and ratify them.
I would like to ask the minister who are the three men in London, who are appointed to carefully pick out of the group nominated by Mr. Scateherd men to be enumerators for that district.

I do not understand the minister saying: ' It may be true or it may not be true.' It is plainly evident that Mr. Scateherd was appointed to select the men according to his judgment, and he was compelled to turn over to George M. Reid the names of those 'whom he had chosen; and the minister must know that Mr. Reid is not a fit man to take charge of taking the census in that district. I was sorrv to hear the minister

trying to make the House believe that he did not know what was going on about the Prince Albert election at all. No man knows better about these things than he does. He has had it drummed into him across the floor of this House as to how these frauds are carried on. I was surprised that he should try to lead the House to believe that he had heard nothing of it, and also try to belittle the member from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) for bringing forward a matter of national importance to the people of Canada. I sincerely hope the minister will see his way clear to support this resolution and thus help us to make sure that the men connected with the Census Department are free from political bias.

speechtext:
I have not followed this debate closely, nor am I familiar with the facts brought forward during this discussion, but I would avail myself of this opportunity to get from the government a clear declaration in regard to the opinion enunciated by my hon. friend from Moose-jaw (Mr. Knowles) who stated here that the government would not tell us the basis or the recommendation on which these enumerators were appointed in different constituencies. I think we are entitled to know whether that is the policy of the government, and whether they intend to act upon that principle. My hon. friend stated here:	We are governing the country, we are in possession of power, we will satisfy ourselves as to the nomination of these enumerators, and you shall not know upon what basis they are appointed. Is that the principle upon which the government will act in the eastern as well as in the western portions of Canada? The Minister of Agriculture said the other day, in answer to an inquiry, that he was satisfied as to the qualification of an enumerator, and that he would not state who had recommended that man. Is that going to be the policy? If so, I think in the face of the. declaration made here to-night by the member for Moosejaw, that we are entitled to a statement from the minister on behalf of the government.
What are the facts? Is it my hon. friend who pays for the cost of the census, or is it the people of Canada? Everybody knows that the minister in charge of the department does not himself know of the persons qualified to act in each electoral district. My hon. friend knows that, and will admit it. He is, therefore, obliged to seek outside information and, as a matter of fact, fwe all know that under the detestable and damnable system of patronage which prevails in this country the appointment is made upon the recommendation of whom? Of a political partisan, of a friend who makes the recommendation, somebody
generally in the electoral division who has some personal purpose to serve. That, I suppose, is inevitable. But are we going to be told that the House of Commons, in its general inquisitorial power, will be refused information as to the reasons which guided the minister in making the appointment, that we will not be told upon whose recommendation he assumes responsibility for that appointment? Such a proposition is preposterous, and in the face of the declaration made to-night by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) and applauded by the minister in his quiet little way, by slapping his desk, we are entitled to know whether that is the principle which is to guide the government. Was that the principle that governed in Quebec where some appointments have been approved of, and some are found very unwise? What was the motive, what was the recommendation that guided executive action? We are told that when governments get old they get faulty; I have read that in many places, and it has been said that among other things they profess that they are the masters, that they are the possessors of power, not the trustees of the people. We could have no better evidence of that than this refusal. I still believe that the government will not lay down the principle that we are not entitled to that information, but I would like to know the principle that is going to guide the government.

speechtext: One or two names have been mentioned here to-night in connection with the forthcoming census that I think call for a word or two from me, because I know some of the gentlemen who have been named. I know the career of Mr. Reid in the past as a politican. As the Minister of Agriculture knows, Mr. Reid was directly connected with the notorious Elgin frauds. His name was a household word, with that of O'Gorman, in connection with these frauds. He was later connected with O'Gorman, in the no less notorious London election frauds, which led to the resignation of a colleague of the minister. If the hon. gentleman thinks he can put his head into the sand and escape observation, escape opprobrium and contempt, by professing toot to know who these men are, I tell him he is mistaken. The people of Canada know the history of those notorious cases, and they know that the minister is aware of every fact and detail, and yet the men who have been mentioned here are allowed to take part in making appointments upon the taking of the census.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
The taking of our census is not a mere formal or frivolous matter; it is a very important matter. The statistics gathered by these enumerators

will determine the representation in this House, and guide us in many other very important matters during the next decade, and it must appear to every member of this House that it is of the utmost importance that these statistics should be gathered in such a manner, and by such persons, as to command the utmost confidence of every man in Canada. I quite agree with the observations of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) when he finds fault with the position taken by the Minister of Agriculture. That hon. minister tells us:	I do not pretend to know the
enumerators whom I have appointed. If he were in a position to give his word that he knew every one of them, and knew every one to be sufficiently intelligent, and to be men of character, perhaps we would be satisfied with his wTord; but he does not tell us that. He tells us he does not know one of these enumerators whom he has appointed, and in the face of that he refuses to tell us upon whose recommendation he appoints these men. These men are to do important work for the whole people of Canada. They are to be paid out of funds which are the moneys of the people of Canada, and the people's -representatives in this House, I submit, have a right to know upon whose recommendation he appoints them. He has admitted to us this afternoon, if I understood him aright, that he has appointed several men to the important position of enumerators, on recommendations made by this man Perry, and every moderate man will admit at once upon the evidence adduced on this motion that Perry is not a proper man, not a man of sufficient character to warrant the Minister of Agriculture in accepting his recommendation for the appointment of any enumerator. I could understand very well the Minister of Agriculture saying: Heretofore I supposed that Mr. Perry was a man of unblemished character.
I am satisfied upon the evidence I have heard here to-night that he is not; I will make further inquiry to ascertain the standing and character of the men I have appointed upon his recommendation before I permit them to go to work. Would not that be a reasonable position for the Minister of Agriculture to take, if, as he tells us, up to this moment, he never knew anything against the character of Mr. Perry? 'T.his is not the only case in which the taking of the census is being used for party purposes. This seems to be not the only case in which men are appointed enumerators upon the recommendation of worthless characters like Perry. It must appeal to all as it appeals to me, that the enumerators shall be men of character, men of intelligence, men whose work will be accepted freely by the people of this country as having been honestly and in-Mr. CROTHERS
telligently done. If such men are not employed the census will be utterly useless. The census will be a valuable thing if taken on a scientific basis by competent men, but if it is taken, as appears from this case and the London case, by party heelers as a reward for party services, then the government need not be disappointed if they find that the people have no confidence whatever ih the results of the work of the enumerators. One or two of my friends have referred to this man Reid, and I should like also to refer to him for a moment also. It seems that Mr. E. W. Scatcherd has been appointed commissioner by this government for the city of London, and as I understand it was the *duty of the commissioner to select the enumerators. I could understand the Minister of Agriculture selecting as a commissioner a man of reputation and character, whom he could trust to select competent and intelligent enumerators to work under him. What do we find this man Scatcherd doing? If the articles in the newspapers are correct, we find Scatcherd actually stating to the London 'Evening Free Press' that he handed over the names of all these one hundred and five applicants to G. M. Reid for him to determine who, if any, of those 105 men should be appointed to act as enumerators for the city of London. Gould a greater outrage be perpetrated upon the people of London and the people of this country? Who is George M. Reid? The Minister of Agriculture said a few minutes ago that he would not recognize any charges made in newspapers or letters, even when, facsimiles of the originals are produced. He wanted something proved in court. Well, this man, George M. Reid, has been in court. We all remember that very shortly after the passing of Bills establishing the new provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, we had a bye-election in the city of London, and the result of that election was a majority in favour of the government. We had it proclaimed from one end of this country to the other that this was a test of public opinion as to the Bills which had been carried by this House establishing these two provinces. What followed that? It was established in the police court of Toronto, not in the newspapers, that in one corner, one subdivision, of the city of London, because there was only one man who squealed who handled the money, 100 men had been bought at the price of $10 apiece, less a rake-off of fifty cents that was taken by the man who made the payments. That is how that bye-election was carried, that is how that 'large majority was obtained in favour of the Bills establishing the new provinces of Saskatchewan ana Alberta. What followed that? Four men were arrested and indicted for conspiracy. One of the four was George M. Reid. These four

men were tried before His Honour Judge Winchester, the senior judge for the county of York, and convicted of conspiracy; yet George M. Reid is the man to whom the commissioner appointed by the Minister of Agriculture hands over the names to make the selection of those who are to make the enumeration. Of course, I do not state it as a fact that the commissioner handed these names over; I am saying that that is what is stated by this newspaper. I do not want to be misunderstood as to that. What confidence can the people of Canada have in a census taken in that way? We have a gentleman at the head of the department having control of the census saying: I will not tell you upon whose recommendation I have made these appointments; I have made them upon the recommendation of men whose character and standing were satisfactory to me. He does not get up and say:	I will rectify the
wrong, if there is any, I will inquire further as to the character of these men whom I have appointed on the recommendation of Mr. Perry, I will instruct Mr. Scatcherd that that is not the way in which I want the census taken; I do not approve of my commissioner handing over the names of the applicants to a man who has been convicted of fraud, of a serious offence against the election laws of this country. But, he does not take a position of that kind. I refuse to tell you who recommended these enumerators. It is a party matter; the hon. member for Moose-jaw'(Mr. Knowles) says; it is none of your business; we are doing this work on our side of the House; we are allowing such men as Perry chooses to be appointed as enumerators, a man who, upon his own confession, is of the character we have heard described here this evening. We are accepting the recommendation of this man who has been convicted in a court of justice of defrauding the electors of London. We are doing this work, it is none of your business., and we propose to continue it in this way. I ask what confidence the people of Canada can have in a census being taken in that vTay and costing over a million dollars?

speechtext:
I believe the people of Canada mil condemn the Minister of Agriculture and this government for not accepting the resolution of my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) which simply declares for clean politics in the taking of the census and the appointment of census officers. The Minister of Agriculture occupied his present position in 1901 when the census was taken, and more than once was he condemned for allowing politics to interfere in a matter which should be free from politics. I have here a letter written to the Minister of Agriculture after the taking of the last_ census by Mr. Kelly, who was census commissioner
for the county of Peterborough, and that letter, together with the circumstances attending it, show the Minister of Agriculture in an unenviable light. Mr. Kelly had an account for $653.14 which was large in comparison with the accounts of the other commissioners, and the department refused to pay it, but Mr. Kelly knew how to reach the Minister of Agriculture, and this is the letter he wrote to him:
The Ontario elections are coming off the end of May or the beginning of June. Mr. B. 0. Lott is the unanimous choice of the Liberal convention. I have made up my mind to do some hard work in this north riding of Hastings. Mr. Lott is the best canvasser and the hardest worker ever went into a political contest.
I have the honour to remain,
Your old servant, WM. KELLY.
Well, Mr. Kelly came down to Ottawa, and he brought with him Mr. Lott, who was the Liberal candidate for the legislature in the county of Hastings, and these two gentlemen interviewed the minister, and after Mr. Kelly went home he wrote this letter, and the account was paid at once.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Did anybody here see Kelly?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Oh, yes, the Minister of Agriculture saw Kelly, but Lott went to the United States and has not returned. You will remember that this was the same Mr. Lott who was interested in the ballot box stuffing case in the province of Ontario, and that is the company Mr. Kelly was in. The Minister of Agriculture talks about there being no politics in the taking of the census, but let me rgad to the minister the following advertisement in the Elora * Express ' of Wednesday, February 8, 1911:
