speechtext:
Notice of Meeting.
A meeting of the Liberal Association of the township of Pilkington will he held on Friday, the 10th of February, 1911,
At Three o'clock P.M.
At the residence of the undersigned in Elora, for the purpose of naming census enumerators for the township of Pilkington.
THOS. MARSHALL, President.
Elora, Jan. 31, 1911.
Elora is the constituency of South Wellington, and the Minister of Agriculture knows that this meeting was held, and he has in his office the very men who were named at this political meeting. He won't deny that he appointed the men whose names were sent in from that meeting. Do we want any further proof that there is politics in the taking of the census? I do not condemn the Minister of Agriculture for taking recommendations from his own political support-

ers. It is a well known principle pretty generally observed that the government in power take recommendations from their supporters in this House and from the defeated Libera] candidates. That is fairly well defined policy in this country, but the Minister of Agriculture is not living up to that. In order to broaden the influence of the political machine he takes his recommendations from the Reform organizer of the province of Manitoba. Will the Minister of Agriculture say that Mr. Perry was the defeated candidate in the last election, or will he deny that Mr. Perry has the patronage for not only one but several counties in Manitoba? If Mr. Perry were a defeated candidate, I do not know that the House would complain if the Minister of Agriculture adopted his recommendations, because the principle would be fair and I do not think there would be any criticism from this side of the House. But Mr. Perry was not the defeated candidate in the constituency of Macdonald, and the charge is that fhe minister goes outside his supporters in this House and outside the defeated Liberal candidates and receives recommendations. The policy laid down by the hon. gentleman from Moosejaw is fair enough, but the Minister of Agriculture went outside of that policy in order that the political machine in Manitoba should be brought into operation. Not satisfied to take in .the machine in one county, the Minister of Agriculture wants the whole machinery of the Grit party in Manitoba introduced so as to bring political influences to bear in order that the lists in Manitoba and the census in Manitoba shall be prepared in a way that will best help the Reform party in that province. We are suspicious of the Minister of Agriculture for another reason, and that is that before he came into office he preached economy, yet, the census taken under his direction in 1901 cost extravagantly more than the census taken in 1891, when his Conservative predecessor was head of the department. May I illustrate this by showing that in the county of Halton, in 1901, although the population had decreased by 2,437 as compared with the previous census, the cost of taking the census in that county was increased by $1,043.96, and sixteen more enumerators than in the previous census. In the county of South Perth there was a decrease in the population of 1,539, but it cost $1,136.90 more than the previous census, and there were nine more officers appointed. In the county of Peel the popnlation had decreased 1,779, hut the cost increased $865.28, and six more officials than previously were appointed. In the county of Cardwell, although the population had decreased by 2,322, the cost increased by $853.94, and the number of officials by eleven. In the county of Prince Edward the population decreased 1,025, but Mr. BLAIN
under the administration of the present Minister of Agriculture the cost had increased by $1,011.91, and he appointed thirteen more enumerators than were found necessary in 1891. This shows that my hon. friend has adopted, the policy that when the population decreases the cost of taking the census increases. That is a policy that the people of this country knew nothing about until my hon. friend came into office. This is the reason why my hon. friend's department, especially in connection with the taking of the census, is surrounded with so much suspicion. It would have been to the credit of my hon. friend if, when -this Prince Albert matter, with all its corruption, was referred to, he had stood up and said, as a minister of the Crown I have no defence for this, and I will condemn it. That is what we should have expected of my hon. friend, if we had not known him quite so well as we do. As my hon. friend has failed to measure up to what the people of this country would expect in an hon. gentleman occupying so important a position, hfi must take the consequences when he refuses to adopt so reasonable a resolution as that moved by my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples).

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize one matter that has not been very clearly brought out in the course of the debate. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture spoke of this notice as one which had been sent out apparently in quite an incidental way by Mr. H. E. Perry, who happens to be the Liberal organizer for the province of Manitoba. I would like to point out to him that this document certainly bears on its face the evidence of wholesale work of this character throughout that province. It bears the printed heading:	'Manitoba
Liberal Executive, Organizer's Office, P.O. Drawer 2076, Winnipeg, Canada.' Then the circular is filled in by some kind of a machine, leaving blank spaces for three particulars-the name of the man and his post office address, the name of the constituency, and the description of the census enumeration division for which he is to foe appointed. The circular bears a stamped signature. Any one who looks at it for a moment can see that it is stamped. So that this is simply one of perhaps thousands of these notices that have gone out in the province of Manitoba from Mr. P< r-ry. That is perfectly obvious from the slightest perusal of this document. So that there can be no question or doubt that this notice is a part of a system under which hundreds and perhaps thousands have been sent throughout the province of Manitoba. Does my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture deny that? I will submit this to the judgment of any one of his supporters

in this House and ask him to say that the perusal of the document will not bear out what I am saying. A little slip is attached to indicate the census enumeration division; there is a blank for the man's name and a blank for the federal constituency, all indicating a system by which these appointments have in effect been made by the Liberal organizer for the province of Manitoba.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: And in every other province too.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
I do not know about any other province, but we have the evidence here of what has been done ii the province of Manitoba. Now, it has been very well said to-night that the census is an exceedingly important event in our national life, and that the people of this country have the right to demand that it shall be taken fairly. They have also the right to demand that the public money of this country shall not be paid out for party purposes under the pretense of a census enumeration. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has been rather lordly about this matter. We have heard the doctrine proclaimed in this House this evening that this government is in power, and that they can act on the recommendation of criminals in the penitentiary if they see fit ; that it does not lie in the mouths of gentlemen on this side of the House, or in the mouth of any citizen in Canada, to raise the slightest objection thereto, because Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government are in power, and they can act as they see fit, and do what they like with the public money of this country. That seems to he the theory of these gentlemen. Let us for a moment examine the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture with regard to this particular gentleman selected to make appointments in the province of Manitoba. We heard something this afternoon about trivial offences. Apparently, in the eyes of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, it is only a trivial matter, worthy of only passing notice, that two deputy returning officers and their poll clerk should go into that northern country, should pretend to hold a poll, should violate their oath of office, should violate every provision of the Election Act, should sit in the wilderness and write in 150 names of fictitious persons, should place 150 false ballots in the ballot box, should sign and swear to false returns as to the poll having been held, and should bring all these statements back as if that poll had been actually held in good faith under the election law. I do not know one provision of the election law that they did not violate, in addition to which as I have already said, they have been guilty of forgery and perjury. There does not seem to be any 286
dispute about the facts. They were brought out not only in court, but as' I understand, before the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan. Now, what is the position of Mr. Perry with regard to this? I will not go over the letters; they have been read over and over again. I just want to refer to one or two passages. A letter of October 4, 1906, from Mr. Perry to one of these men who were absent in the United States:	*
I would suggest extreme caution; I shall try to keep you advised.
The ' Standard ' here last night published a story that, if the ease went against Sinclair, lie was going to squeal, but I don't believe that, as he would never do anything to help the Tories; he is too sore on them.
Indicating a distinct knowledge on the part of the man who wrote that letter, not only that these crimes had been committed with which they had been charged, but that there were other crimes as to which there was a danger that Mr. Sinclair might speak. A letter of June 10:
I have heard it said that the missing deputies would be as well to keep out of sight. I think this is undoubtedly correct.
Further on, in a letter of the next day:
Prudence would, I should judge, suggest to the absent deputies that their safety lies in remaining away.	r
Another letter, which does not appear to have been actually from Perry, but from a gentleman who was associated with him in bringing aid and comfort to them:
Everybody is prepared to stand by their guns and do what is right by you, and what I ask is that you hold steady for a while longer until all can be arranged.
What does that mean? That means that these men have been sent away to the United States by the connivance and with the money of some person or persons. It means that these men have been kept in the United States at the suggestion and by means of the money of certain persons. Further on this letter says:
See Mark, and he will fix things up with you.
Who is Mark? If you turn to the first letter here, you will find who he is. He is Mr. Mark Sands of the firm of Sands and Scott, to whom letters intended for these gentlemen were sent in order that their address might not be known to any one in Prince Albert. What further does this gentleman say? He says:-
See Mark, and he will fix things up with you. Thought best to send it that way.
What is the meaning of ' it ' ? ' It,' as I understand, is the ' wherewithal which enabled these men to remain in the United States when the hand of criminal justice



should have fastened on them in Canada long before. These were the lawyers in [DOT]Chicago to whom letters were sent intended for these absconding and criminal deputies in order that the whereabouts of the absconders might be kept secret. But these were trivial offences and trivial matters which impressed themselves so little upon the Minister of Agriculture that although he heard them referred to at length at least twice in this House, he has entirely forgotten them this afternoon and apparently never heard of them before. Were these transactions so much in the ordinary course of affairs that imy hon. friend was not impressed by them? Let nre tell him the position which Perry occupied in this connection. Has my hon. friend never heard of such a thing as an accessory after the fact. Here is a definition in the Criminal Code,-section 71:-
An accessory after the fact to an offence is one who receives, comforts or assists anybody who has been a party to such an offence in order to enable him to escape, knowing him to be a party thereto.
I say that if these letters are genuine- and if they are not genuine this man has had his remedy for a year or more in the public courts of this country-in my opinion Mr. Perry was an accessory after the fact to the crimes that those men had committed and as to their participation in which there can be no reasonable doubt. When we find the virtual appointment of the census renumerators in Manitoba committed to that gentleman under those circumstances, I think it is more than right that my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) should have risen to vindicate common honesty and decency in this country by moving the motion which he has made and which I shall be most happy to support.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

Much has been said of matters important in themselves but not really relating to the census, so that there is danger of our losing sight of the real circumstances and methods under which the census has to be taken. There are two classes of census officials. There are the commissioners, who have charge of the different counties or electoral districts, one to each district. Numbers of the commissioners have been appointed, but throughout this debate no attempt has been made to show that any one has been chosen who is not worthy and qualified to perform the service. Then we have the enumerators, a much more numerous class, because each enumerator has charge of a comparatively small subdivision. These run into the thousands and have been in many cases already appointed or are in course of being appointed from day to day. Throughout all this discussion it has not been charged that any man has been chosen as enumerator Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
who is not qualified for the work, who is not respectable and reputable in every sense of the word.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: We do not know them yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Then my hon. friend should not be so ungenerous as to cast any reflection upon them. He should wait until he finds some reason to criticise the appointments of the commissioners or enumerators.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Might I put a question? If it be true, as charged in the newspapers, that the commissioner appointed for the city of London, handed the names of the applicants into the hands of Mr. Reid to decide who should be appointed, does the hon. minister think the commissioner who would do this was a worthy man to hold the position.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I am not aware of the circumstances, but generally speaking if any commissioner should put his list of the names into the hands of anybody and give him any control in the appointment, I would not consider he was acting wisely or properly. I do not, however, know anything more about this than my hon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Crothers) knows himself, but I want to call attention to these essential facts. Mr. Perry is a commissioner or enumerator and has no official connection whatever with the government or with the taking of the census, and, therefore, the outcry raised concerning him has no bearing on the question as to whether we are appointing reputable men to be commissioners or census enumerators.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Does the hon. minister know that Mr. Perry according to the statement of the Minister of Agriculture, has been recommending enumerators to those positions? .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. gentleman in all sincerity that I know no more about it than what I have heard in this debate to day. As to the question of recommendations, I shall come to that in a moment. But I want again to emphasize the fact that the commissioners and the enumerators are the only people who have to do with the census. The Minister of Agriculture must take the responsibility of those appointments. When he has to appoint thousands of men all over Canada, no doubt among them he may appoint some whom our hon. friends opposite will find reason to criticise, but there is so far no allegation that any commissioner or any enumerator has been improperly appointed. That being the case, how can hon. gentleman opposite hope to influence public opinion by reviving the old story

of the Prince Albert election; I am not referring to that as a trivial matter. It was a grave and serious matter, and I do not complain if hon. gentlemen offer any condemnation of what occurred at that time. When we come to the question of recommendation, hon. gentlemen opposite lay down the proposition that it is the duty of the government to declare on whose representation any one has been appointed to a public office. But on reflection they must see that such a theory is preposterous. Take the appointment of a lieutenant governor of a province, will any hon. gentleman opposite contend that he has the right to demand in this House and to know on whose recommendation such an appointment was made? Every member of this House has of course the right to put a question, but must be guided by reason and propriety, and would it be reasonable and proper to ask on whose recommendation the appointment of a lieutenant governor of any province was made? Take the appointment of a judge. Could anything be more ridiculous than to insist on knowing who recommended his appointment? Will the hon. member for Jacques Cartier stand up and say that he has the right to know who made the recommendation?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I never put forth such an absurd proposition. What I said was that the nomination of such officers as enumerators could only he made upon recommendation as a basis, and it was the right of every member to know what that basis was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: And the nomination of a lieutenant governor could only be made upon a basis. There is no difference in principle between the appointment of a high officer and the nomination of an officer of a lower grade. If it was a governor, he would not ask who recommended him. If it was a judge, he would not do anything so preposterous as to insist upon knowing who recommended him. Well, if he is a census commissioner who is appointed, would it be less preposterous for him to ask who recommended him?

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Why you appointed him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
Because we needed a man for the office and our information was that he was a suitable man. And that is the reason why we appointed the Governor -because we needed a man for the office and our information was that he was a suitable man. And that is just the reason why we appoint a judge-because the place had to be filled and our information was that the gentleman in question was well qualified by his legal attainments to fill the office. Hon. gentlemen opposite cannot be serious in advancing the argument that 286 i
it is the right of the House to be informed what are our grounds for-

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: What harm will it do?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
But the hon. gentleman must permit us to be the judges. The House has rights, and these rights we do not question. But hon. members opposite have an unhappy faculty of speaking of what the House demands when what they mean is what they themselves ask. Nobody in this House would question for a moment the right of the House to demand information in the proper way. But when an hon. member stands up in the House and insists upon the right to obtain certain information, I think it does not necessarily follow that he has that right in the sense in which he uses the word.
Now, much has been said throughout this discussion of nominations by political committees. I am bound to say that, while I do not think the political committee is the best way of doing the thing, and while I do not like it myself and would discourage it, I am not prepared to admit that there is anything wrong in having a political committee make a recommendation to any minister in regard to an appointment in which the members of that committee may be interested. They cannot be denied the right to make a recommendation in a public matter. The field of party patronage is, I am glad to sav, being somewhat narrowed, there is less of it under this government than there ever was under any of its predecessors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
There is less room for the exercise of party patronage to-day than there was in any previous time in the history of Canada. But, so long as we have party government-and, with all its evils it seems to be about the best system that can be devised,-it is inevitable that there will be more or less of what is called party patronage; there will be a human desire on the part of every government to give the preference to their friends. Just at present, the census being about to be taken, my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has a right to make a selection of the officers to take that census, getting the best information that he can. And, twenty years hence, we will concede to hon. gentlemen opposite a similar privilege. And those of us who are here then may question and may find fault in other respects, but will not deny their right tq appoint their own friends to office, always with the qualification that the men appointed must be reputable men and able to fulfil the duties for which they are appointed. Even if the committee was used, it would not be a reasonable ground for criticism, although J confess I do not like the system

Hon. gentlemen opposite complain that, in making appointments in counties represented by hon. members on this side, we turn to the member for advice in the matter. As to counties represented by hon. gentlemen opposite with whatever gravity they try to discuss this question, they cannot expect us to go and ask their advice. Well, if we have to get information in reference to an appointment in a county represented by an hon. member sitting on that side of the House, surely the minister in charge of the department concerned must be left to exercise his own judgment and discretion as to the manner in which he will get that information; and, for the judgment he shall exercise he is accountable to the House and the country

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: In the case of the enumerator in the county referred to or in the appointment of an excise officer, is not the sitting member entitled to know on whose recommendation he is appointed, since he is not consulted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: According to the conception of government that I have-which, I think, is that held by every government that has ever held office in this country^ my hon. friend would not have the right to ask that. It would make no difference who recommends it, the minister must be responsible, and if the persons appointed by the minister prove to be improper persons and unfit for their duty, the minister would have to bear the responsibility, and his colleagues would have to share it with him. And I do not think, that on reflection, hon. gentlemen opposite will gravely adhere to the view tnat it is the duty of the minister to tell at a given moment on what recommendation any officer of the census, or judge or governor is appointed to office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: There is just the difference. In the case just referred to, the member on the government side gets that knowledge, whereas a member on this side of the House he does not know, and the public is not entitled to know, and therefore there is nobody known to be responsible for the recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: Yes, the minister who makes the appointment is responsible and the government that endorse it is responsible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) himself has given the strongest argument and the best reason why the principle laid down by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) ought to govern appointments of this nature. He himself has stated that it is utterly impossible for the Minister of Agriculture, making such a large number of appointments all over the Dominion, to Mr. FIELDING.
personally know the individual character of his appointee. And that was the basis of the argument of the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that the House has a right to know the basis on which appointments are made, in order that we may thereby judge the character of the appointments. And the whole argument on this side this afternoon is based exactly on that principle. I think the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) had the right to bring the question into the House, and his right is based on that very principle. I think it was argued rightly by the Minister of Finance that if there was no connection between the letters read here and the appointments made, our case falls to the ground. But the hon. member for Macdonald laid the foundations for his argument carefully and well. He started out by reading a document which, I think, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has made very clear, was an official document; he has sliov.n that it was a circular, not an individual letter, issued by an irresponsible person, on an official letterhead and bearing the title of an official organization. There were blank spaces left for filling in essential particulars, and these had been filled in the letter submitted. I will call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that, if further evidence were wanting that this was an official document recognized not only by the government but directly by the Minister of Agriculture it was given in the admission made by the Minister of Agriculture himself during this debate. He stated in answer to the question put from this side that he had acted on the recommendation of this Mr. Perry and in some cases had appointed enumerators on the recommendation of that gentleman.
He did not tell us how many he had appointed on his recommendation, but the whole inference of the letters, and the written evidence produced in the House makes it a prima facie case that he has been acting generally in an official manner in making these various recommendation!?. I was glad t-o know that the Minister of Firiance himself said that he did not look upon that as a very trifling matter, that it was a very serious charge that had been made against these gentlemen. He admitted they had been guilty of certain criminal offences, and I think the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has clearly demonstrated that the man who is making these appointments or on whose recommendations the appointments were made, and who has undertaken officiallv to notify these men of their appointments, of their duties, the amount they are to receive, and the particular territory over which they would have jurisdiction, has been acting semi-offieially. The leader of

the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has clearly shown that the man was accessory after the fact to the crimes committed at that time. That being the case, we have a right to bring up this question in order that the country at large may know the basis on which these various appointments are made, and how much confidence we should place in enumerators or officials acting on behalf of this government who are gathering statistics which are of vital importance to this country. The census will cost about $1,000,000, but apart from the mere financial cost, the importance of the data we are supposed to secure by the taking of this census, which is of vital importance to the Dominion of Canada, amply justifies the hon. member 'for Macdonald (Mr. Staples) when the information came to him, in bringing it before the House; in fact, it was his bounden duty to do so. I lam amazed that the principle should be laid down by the minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) that he is not prepared to consider evidence of that nature, that he feels he is not bound by his office to give the information to the House to which I think we are entitled. That is the argument, and the position taken by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), and by every member on this side. We are not asking for the individual recommendations that come to hon. members of the government from time to time, but we are asking on what basis or principle appointments of this kind are made, or on what principle the minister judges the recommendations that come to him. These recommendations could not possibly come to the minister in a private way. For instance, if the minister were to resign to-morrow, no man would continue to send in recommendations to him to make appointments for offices of this kind. Therefore, it is wholly and solely in his official position as a minister of the government that these recommendations come to him, and so they are the public property of the people of Canada, they should be placed upon the public files, and should be-at all times at the disposal of this House. He is laying down a wrong principle when he undertakes to say that that is purely a private matter between him and the persons making these recommendations. He has a very wrong conception of his position, and his duty in regard to that question. But it is like many other principles that we constantly find laid down from that side of the House in regard to what they consider the constitutional method of government. I am preparea on the evidence that has been adduced this afternoon, to earnestly support the motion of the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples). I
had heard nothing of this case previously, but I consider the hon. member has made out a most complete case, and that it is the duty of this government to accept the recommendation, and produce letters of this kind. We must accept the minister's word that he has not officially authorized Mr. Perry to send out these circulars, but there is not the slightest doubt that he has received these instructions and authority from some governmental source. The minister shakes his head. Supposing I or any other private citizen to-morrow issued circulars throughout Canada signed personally, to all the enumerators, stating that they had been recommended to the position of enumerators, and that they had certain jurisdiction, giving them the amount of remuneration for their work and asking them to Teport to me within ten days, would he take cognizance of that, or would he immediately take steps to see, in some way that I was prevented sending out circulars of that kind.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext: I would take no notice of it whatever.

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.
speechtext:
That is an amazing statement of the minister that any private citizen could send out in a case of this kind involving the appointment of thousands of officials to be paid for by public money, circulars stating what the duties and remuneration of these officials are to be, and asking them to report in ten days; the minister says he would take no notice of it. It is an amazing statement and one which I scarcely think any business man or any man realizing the responsibility he has in connection with the office he holds, would make.
It is in the context that we find the sting of that circular. Mr. Perry says in a postscript: If you are in the city within a short time, drop in. Why? To talk over with him the good cause, because he signs himself:	Yours in the good .cause.
Every sentence of that carefully worded circular goes to show that it is issued in order to bring political influence to bear. The wording of the circular is such as to impress on the minds of those receiving it that they have received their appointments through the influence of the Liberal association, whose printed official statement is on the head of the paper on which the letter is written. So before we commence to take the census at all, we find held out to the people of Canada that it is to be purely a political institution used for political purposes, and I ask in the face of 'that how are the people of this country to have confidence in a census taken in that manner?

when the Minister of Finance lectured this side of the House on the question and said that hon. members had not proven that a single criminal had been appointed a commissioner, I was surprised. He is prepared to take it all. He has not even the Minister of Finance to help him. The Minister of Finance says that not one of the enumerators is a criminal. We do not know these men, we do not know what they are going to do, but we do know that if we accent the recommendations of men of this character we are going to get into a bad condition with regard to the census. of Agriculture in the selection of these enumerators have been criminals. He said at one time that it did not make any difference what was said about any man as long as it was1 not proved in court. WESTERN COAL STRIKE. Conciliation Board can't Agree and Adjourns.
Fernie, B.C., May 13.-The Dominion Conciliation Board, which is trying to settle the strike of ten thousand western miners, has declared that nothing can be done at present, as the members are so divided in their views, and the Board has adjourned sine die.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the House to the fact that the report is being industriously circulated by certain news-

papers that the opposition is pursuing a course of obstructive tactics in this House in connection with the debate on reciprocity, and that the effect will be to prevent the Prime Minister from attending the imperial conference. That the report is without a shadow of foundation is well known to every member of this House, and to every newspaper reporter in the press gallery. Notwithstanding this, respectable and even religious newspapers industriously circulated the falsity. One of the offenders in this respect is the ' Christian Guardian,' the organ of the great Methodist church. If this were its first offence it might be overlooked, but unfortunately for the paper, and the church it represents, it is continuously misrepresenting the facts. Editorially it makes the following statement in its issue of May 3:

maintopic: SUPPLY-EXPERIMENTAL FRUIT AND VEGETABLE FARMS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

speechtext:
Just now one of the livest questions at Ottawa is whether Canada shall be represented at the Imperial Conference by Sir Wilfrid Laurier or not. The Conservative tactics in opposing the reciprocity pact are such as to greatly delay the passing of the measure, and there seems not to be any too good reason to hope that there will be a change in the situation. The Conservatives are determined that the reciprocity pact shall not be ratified without a general election; and the Liberals are determined it shall, if at all possible. Our rules of procedure, fortunately or unfortunately, allow what we may call obstructionist tactics to be carried to a very great length, and the Conservatives are determined to light every step of the way. Unfortunately, however, this is Coronation year, and also the year of the Imperial Conference, and if the fight over the reciprocity pact is continued it will be impossible for Canada to be properly represented at either. From every standpoint this would seem to be most unfortunate. For Canada, the greatest British colony, to be unrepresented or inadequately represented, at either the conference or the Coronation, would appear little less than unseemly. Both parties realize this, and yet neither is willing to yield a jot to its opponent. We cannot but hope, however, that the cooler and wiser heads in the two parties will succeed in reaching some wav out of the difficulty. It will not be complimentary to our Canadian parliament if they do not.
When the reciprocity proposition was introduced in this House, the statement was made by the Prime Minister and bv the Finance Minister that the _ fullest time and opportunity would be given to discuss the question in this House. The Finance Minister was most emphatic in this. On February 9, 1911, page 3358, he said:
There will be abundant opportunity for the members of this House and the people of this country to carefully consider the arrangement to which the government asks them to give their approval.
On page 3360 the Finance Minister said:
But we propose to proceed with this measure not rashly but in due order.
On March 8, 1911, on page 4947, he said:
We desire that this matter shall be discussed, as I stated in the earlier stages of the debate, not hastily, not in a rush, not unduly; we desire that every member of the House shall have abundant opportunity to form and express his views.
Thus it will be seen that there was to be ample time for a very full discussion of the subject. Members on both sides of the House have presented their views. Those on the government side have taken their full share of the time that has up to the present been occupied in the debate. No obstructive tactics of any kind have been introduced by the opposition. On the con trary, Mr. Borden, the opposition leader, has made it plain that there will be no obstacle thrown in the way of the Prime Minister's attendance at the Coronation and the imperial conference.	_	.
In order that there may be no mistake m this matter, I will read what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) said on the floor of the House on the 28th day of Apri., which was five days before the article was published which I have read from the 'Christian Guardian',:
I am very happy indeed to concur in the hope which he has expressed that he may be enabled to attend the approaching Imperial Conference.	'	, .
Now, there are three courses which would permit the Prime Minister to attend the approaching Imperial Conference. If the present session of parliament should not have come to a conclusion at the time when it will be necessary for him to leave, he could proceed to the conference, leaving his colleagues m charge of the business of the House; that is one alternative as to the desirability or expediency of which I am not so good a judge as the Prime Minister himself. I frankly concede that that is a matter upon which it is his right, his duty, to exercise his own judgment. In the second place, he can bring the session to an end, leaving some of these very important matters unfinished and letting them stand over to another session. It has alreadv been intimated to us that the Bank Act will not be pressed at the present session. If that is to stand over to another sessiop, there can be no particular reason why the proposals for closer trade relations with the United States should not also stand over until another session. I do not want to enter into any controversial observations with regard to that, I only mention it as another alternative which is open to the Prime Minister in that regard. Then in the third place, he can adjourn this session of parliament for two or three months, or whatever length of time may be sufficient to enable "lm to attend the Imperial Conference and the Coronation. After the Coronation and after the conference, the session can be resumed; and I desire to say now that for the purpose of facilitating

public business we would be prepared to give interim supply to such an extent as the public interest would demand, in case the Prime Minister should see fit to follow that course.
Every member on this side of the House is willing and anxious that the Prime Minister should attend the Coronation and the Imperial Conference, and are willing to make any sacrifice to this end. As yet not one-half the members on the Conservative side of the House have had an opportunity to express their views on the reciprocity pact. Nearly all of those who have not yet spoken have made preparation so to do, but are willing that the House should adjourn in order that Canada may be properly represented by the Prime Minister at the Imperial Conference. In view of these facts, which the editor of the 'Christian Guardian' must have known, it seems very much out of place that he should have penned the article he did, which appeared in the issue of that journal, of May 3. I have waited for several days, hoping that the editor in last week's issue.might make a correction, but he has not done so. I regret very much that the ' Guardian ' should be made the organ of misrepresentation, and I hope that the editor may be honest enough to correct the wrong he has done in his next issue.

The grain exhibit also comes from nearly all the provinces, although wheat naturally comes largely from the Northwest and Ontario.
